findings.title: Two CI steps can never execute a single test; they fail for the wrong reason
findings.evidence: Root vitest.config.ts includes only src/** and packages/shared/src/**. CI line 55 runs `npx vitest run backend/tests/...` from the repo root -> 'No test files found, exiting with code 1'. CI line 98's second command runs after `cd backend`, so src/contracts/reports.dfp015.test.ts is matched against the backend config's tests/** glob -> also 'No test files found', exit 1.
findings.actual: Both steps exit 1 having run zero tests. The migration-journal and schema-parity guards they exist to enforce never execute.
findings.expected: Each step runs from the directory whose vitest config covers the tests it names.
findings.downstream_effects: Migration journal drift and schema/PG divergence would reach main undetected.
findings.reproduction: From repo root: npx vitest run backend/tests/migrations-journal-guard.test.ts backend/tests/schema-migration-parity.test.ts ; echo $?  -> 1
findings.existing_test_coverage: None — this is a defect in the gate itself.
findings.recommended_fix: Prefix line 55 with `cd backend && `; move line 98's second command above its `cd backend` or into its own root-level step.
findings.regression_risk: None. Both target files exist on disk (verified with ls).
findings.regression_test: A CI step asserting the string 'No test files found' is absent from output.

findings.title: npm run lint exits 1 with 245 errors plus 50 warnings; repo cannot pass its own CI Lint gate
findings.evidence: `npm run lint` -> '✖ 295 problems (245 errors, 50 warnings)', exit 1. All 245 errors are the prettier/prettier rule. `npx prettier --check .` -> 'Code style issues found in 812 files'.
findings.actual: Lint gate is a hard failure on formatting alone, independent of any code defect.
findings.expected: CLAUDE.md claims 'Lint warnings are at exactly 50 (the limit)' — that describes warnings only and is materially stale; the 245 errors are a separate harder failure the note omits.
findings.downstream_effects: CI Lint job fails; real lint findings are buried under formatting noise.
findings.recommended_fix: Run `npx prettier --write` in a dedicated formatting commit, then re-run the lint gate.
findings.regression_risk: Rewrites 812 files and would bury any functional change in an enormous diff — reformat separately from behaviour changes.

findings.title: FORCE-RLS sweep exempts only revoked_tokens by name; six other tables have a NULLABLE tenant_id
findings.evidence: The loop's only exemption is `c.relname <> 'revoked_tokens'`; it tests that a tenant_id column EXISTS but never `a.attnotnull`. Seven schema tables declare tenantId without .notNull(). Migration 20260929 grants platform_or_tenant policies to five of them (licenses, secrets, server_installations, license_audit_events, setup_wizard_state) — but sync_state has NO policy: a grep for `CREATE POLICY ... ON sync_state` across all migrations and rls/enable-rls.sql returns zero matches.
findings.actual: sync_state (tenant_id is its primary key, one row per tenant) is force-RLS'd with no matching policy; a NULL-tenant row cannot match any tenant_id = NULLIF(...) policy.
findings.expected: A structural exemption (`AND a.attnotnull`) or an explicit platform-table allow-list, not a hard-coded table name.
findings.downstream_effects: Forced tables with no policy return 0 rows to the app role even for the legitimate owner. revoked_tokens had exactly this bug and was fixed by name in 20260927; the same class survives.
findings.reproduction: On a migrated erp_test DB as the NOBYPASSRLS app role with no tenant context: SELECT count(*) FROM sync_state; — 0 rows against a correct database proves the defect.
findings.recommended_fix: Replace the name-based exemption with a structural one or allow-list; add a platform_or_tenant policy for sync_state.
findings.regression_risk: HIGH — the table classification determines which tables the platform role can read. Requires an owner decision.
findings.regression_test: Migration-time assertion, run as the app role, that every FORCE-RLS table has at least one policy.
blockers: No live PostgreSQL contacted — runtime effect NOT VERIFIED

findings.title: Monetary columns passed through a REAL (IEEE-754 float) representation in migration history
findings.evidence: 0024 casts 33 monetary columns to REAL; 0026 then casts them to BIGINT with `USING col::BIGINT`, truncating the already-lossy float; 0036 repeats the BIGINT cast.
findings.actual: Any database live while 0024 was applied had money rounded to ~7 significant digits, then truncated by 0026's cast.
findings.expected: Money is scaled-integer throughout; REAL should never be an intermediate state for a monetary column.
findings.downstream_effects: Potential silent cent-level corruption in financial history on databases migrated through 0024.
findings.reproduction: Inspect any production DB that existed when 0024 applied; compare stored amounts against ledger_entries.
findings.recommended_fix: Owner decision first: determine whether any live DB passed through 0024, then reconcile against ledger_entries. Never apply blind.
findings.regression_test: Row-level reconciliation report, not an automated test.

findings.title: Twelve backend use-case subsystems have no subsystem-named test file
findings.evidence: 20 use-case subsystems, 139 backend test files. No test file names: dashboard, expenses, inventory, notifications, orders, parties, printing, returns, settings, statements, super-admin, vouchers.
findings.actual: No subsystem-named test file exists for these twelve.
findings.expected: METHOD CAVEAT: this is a filename match, not proof of zero coverage — financial-lock-in.test.ts may exercise vouchers and statements without naming them. A content-level check is required before calling any subsystem untested.
findings.downstream_effects: Unknown real coverage in the financial core (vouchers, statements, returns, expenses).
findings.reproduction: Compare directory names under backend/src/application/use-cases/ against backend/tests/*.test.ts filenames.
findings.existing_test_coverage: 0 skipped markers found anywhere (it.skip/it.todo/it.only/describe.skip/xit/xdescribe across backend/tests, backend/src, src, packages/shared/src).
findings.recommended_fix: Content-level audit of each subsystem; add subsystem-named tests where genuinely uncovered.

findings.title: The money arithmetic layer is IEEE-754 float, not scaled-integer
findings.evidence: round2dp(n) { return Math.round((Number.isFinite(n) ? n : 0) * 100) / 100; } — float arithmetic with post-hoc rounding. Storage IS scaled-integer (bigint whole units per the file header), so the defect is confined to arithmetic. A comment at :35-36 explicitly gates any change on an owner decision.
findings.actual: All monetary arithmetic is JS float with one rounding at the end. SYP sums in the 10^10 range stay inside MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, but intermediate products (quantity x unit price, then x exchange rate) can cross it.
findings.expected: Scaled-integer or decimal-string arithmetic so no intermediate product is ever a float.
affected: Every monetary computation routing through round2dp/round4dp/is2dp/hasMoreThan2dp — the whole shared money layer, both engines
findings.downstream_effects: Potential cent-level drift on large SYP sums; bounded in practice by the 2dp rounding.
findings.reproduction: Compute quantity x unit_price x exchangeRate for a large SYP order and compare against scaled-integer arithmetic.
findings.existing_test_coverage: Unknown — the shared money-math test files were reported orphaned by the older audit; not re-verified here.
findings.recommended_fix: Owner decision required — the source comment gates it explicitly. Do not change unilaterally.
findings.regression_risk: HIGH — alters every total in the system; must be reconciled against ledger_entries.
findings.regression_test: Property test over large SYP sums comparing float vs scaled-integer results.

findings.title: POST /orders accepts a financial mutation with no Idempotency-Key
findings.confidence: Confirmed — read directly and compared against nine sibling routes in the same call style.
findings.evidence: order.route.ts:61 uses idempotency("POST") with no { required: true }, while all nine other financial POSTs use { required: true }. The middleware documents the contract at :17-18: 'pass { required: true } on financial mutations so a missing key yields HTTP 428 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REQUIRED'. POST /orders writes the order AND its sync-outbox unit in one transaction (order.route.ts:68-71) and mints the order code from the device's reserved block, so a duplicate is not blocked by a unique constraint on the number.
findings.actual: A request with no Idempotency-Key header is accepted. A retried POST (lost response after commit, or double-tapped submit) creates a second order and a second outbox unit.
findings.expected: idempotency("POST", { required: true }), matching every sibling financial route.
affected: POST /orders only — the single outlier among ten financial mutations
findings.downstream_effects: Duplicate orders produce duplicated stock commitments and duplicated sync-outbox units that propagate to the hub and other devices.
findings.reproduction: curl -X POST /api/orders with a valid body and NO Idempotency-Key header -> expect 428 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REQUIRED, observe 201. Send twice with the same key -> both succeed instead of the second returning the cached response.
findings.existing_test_coverage: Unknown — no test asserting 428 on POST /orders was located.
findings.recommended_fix: Change order.route.ts:61 to idempotency("POST", { required: true }).
findings.regression_risk: BOUNDED BUT REAL — any client POSTing an order without a key starts receiving 428. Audit src/routes/orders.new.tsx and the order API client in src/infrastructure/ for key generation before deploying. All nine other financial routes already require it, so the client very likely sends one — verify, do not assume.
findings.regression_test: Integration test: POST /orders without a key asserts 428; two POSTs with the same key produce exactly one order.

findings.title: HeaderField renders a label with no htmlFor, breaking label/control association on the invoice forms
findings.evidence: HeaderField wraps <Label>{label}</Label> and {children} in sibling <div>s with no htmlFor/id pairing. The underlying Label is Radix-based and DOES forward arbitrary props including htmlFor (src/components/ui/label.tsx spreads {...props} onto LabelPrimitive.Root), so the capability exists and is unused. CLAUDE.md requires FormField 'so the label is tied to its control (htmlFor/useId)'. 14 labelled header fields across the two invoice forms have no programmatic association.
findings.actual: A screen reader announces the input with no name; clicking the label does not focus the control.
findings.expected: HeaderField accepts and forwards an htmlFor, or these fields use FormField as the repo rule requires.
affected: CardField at InvoiceFormLayout.tsx:129 — NOT verified, same pattern suspected
findings.downstream_effects: Accessibility only. Arabic RTL forms with 14 unlabelled inputs is a real barrier for screen-reader users; no data-integrity consequence.
findings.reproduction: Open a new sale invoice, inspect any header field — the <label> has no `for` attribute and the sibling input/select has no matching id.
findings.recommended_fix: Add an optional htmlFor prop to HeaderField and pass it at all 14 call sites, or migrate them to FormField. Check CardField and the two raw <label> checkbox cases in the same pass.
findings.regression_test: A component test asserting every HeaderField renders a <label for> matching its child control's id.

findings.title: POST /users/:id/reset-password enforces only a 6-char minimum and bypasses the PIN-strength rule
findings.evidence: user.route.ts:34 declares `password: z.string().min(6).max(128)`. The repo has a PIN-strength rule enforced at auth.schema.ts:33 (`.refine((pin) => !isWeakPin(pin))`) and setupUseCases.ts:620 (`if (parsed.data.pin && isWeakPin(parsed.data.pin))`), but neither is on the reset-password path.
findings.actual: An admin can reset any user's password to any 6-character string, including isWeakPin-rejected values. The rule is bypassable by choosing a different endpoint.
findings.expected: The reset path applies the same isWeakPin / minimum-length policy as the other credential-setting paths.
findings.downstream_effects: An admin-set weak credential survives every other guard in the system. Classic 'the rule exists but one door does not check it' pattern.
findings.reproduction: As admin: POST /api/users/<id>/reset-password with {"password":"111111"} -> 200. The same value on the PIN-change path is rejected by the isWeakPin refine at auth.schema.ts:33.
findings.recommended_fix: Apply the same isWeakPin refine (or an equivalent strength rule) to the reset-password schema at user.route.ts:34.
findings.regression_risk: Low. RBAC is already correct (rbac(["admin"]) at server.ts:299-306), so this is policy bypass, not missing authorization. Any client setting a 6-char weak password would start receiving 422; the desktop UI is a PIN picker already subject to the stricter rule elsewhere.
findings.regression_test: Test asserting POST /users/:id/reset-password rejects a weak password with 422.

findings.title: dyePurgeRepository hard-DELETEs ledger_entries on PostgreSQL, where the append-only trigger forbids it
findings.evidence: dyePurgeRepository.ts:494 calls .delete(ledgerEntries). The PG trigger 0013_db_hardening.sql:16-19 raises 'ledger_entries is append-only: DELETE not allowed' USING ERRCODE 'insufficient_privilege' on any DELETE. The SQLite twin calls an explicit escape hatch (allowDyePurge -> setFlag('allow_dye_purge')) at sqlite/helpers/dyePurgeRepository.ts:489 before its DELETE. engineHelpers.ts:24-25 dispatches SQLite vs PostgreSQL explicitly. A grep across ALL PG migrations for allow_dye_purge / DISABLE TRIGGER / session_replication_role returns 0 matches.
findings.actual: On the hub engine any dye purge with ledger rows in scope raises insufficient_privilege and the whole transaction rolls back. The same operation succeeds on the desktop SQLite engine.
findings.expected: Either the PostgreSQL path cancels the ledger rows (status -> 'cancelled', which the trigger permits and which 21 other call sites already do), or it has a documented trigger-aware escape hatch matching the SQLite twin.
findings.downstream_effects: Purge is non-functional on the hub and fails LATE — computeDyePurgeImpact (dye.route.ts:62) has already counted the rows it intends to delete, so the impact sheet shown to the user promises a deletion that cannot complete.
findings.reproduction: On a PostgreSQL-backed install with a dye having invoices/returns/vouchers (hence ledger rows) in scope, run the purge -> insufficient_privilege. On SQLite the same purge succeeds. NOT VERIFIED live — no PostgreSQL contacted.
findings.existing_test_coverage: The backend suite defaults to SQLite (npm run test:sqlite), so any existing purge test exercises the WORKING engine. This is precisely the defect class a SQLite-default suite cannot catch.
findings.recommended_fix: Mirror the cancel pattern used by the other 21 call sites — replace the DELETE with a scoped status -> 'cancelled' update — or add a PostgreSQL equivalent of allowDyePurge.
findings.regression_risk: Cancel leaves rows in place, so any downstream count of 'purged' rows and any test asserting the rows are gone must be updated. Reconcile against ledger_entries.
findings.regression_test: A PostgreSQL-engine purge test asserting success and that the ledger rows end status='cancelled'. Must run against PostgreSQL, not only SQLite.

findings.title: /backup/verify-path and /backup/restore-path accept an arbitrary host filesystem path with no directory restriction
findings.evidence: receiveShellPath validates existence (existsSync), file-type (statSync().isFile()), non-emptiness, and an optional size/sha256 match — but never restricts WHICH path may be named. openAndVerifyBackupV3(path, ...) and the restore path then open that arbitrary file. The sha256/sizeBytes checks verify integrity against the caller's own claim, not provenance.
findings.actual: An authenticated admin can name any path on the host and have the server open, hash, parse and report on it; via restore, load an attacker-chosen SQLite file into the live application.
findings.expected: The path should be confined to the application's backup root or an allow-list of sanctioned directories.
findings.downstream_effects: Arbitrary file read (metadata, hash, parse errors leaking path content) and attacker-chosen SQLite loaded via restore. Requires admin credentials.
findings.reproduction: As admin, POST /api/backup/verify-path with {"path":"C:/Windows/System32/config/SAM"} — the server opens and hashes the file instead of rejecting the path.
findings.existing_test_coverage: The dfp028 backup script gate tests the pipeline, not path provenance. No test asserts an out-of-root path is refused.
findings.recommended_fix: Resolve the path and assert it is inside the configured backup root before existsSync; reject otherwise. The desktop shell legitimately hands over a user-picked file (pick_backup_file), so the allow-list must include the OS file-picker's sanctioned location, not only the backup root.
findings.regression_risk: MEDIUM — over-restricting breaks the legitimate 'restore from a user-picked file' desktop flow, which is the entire purpose of the path-based endpoints.
findings.regression_test: A test that a path outside every sanctioned directory is rejected with a distinct error, and that a path inside the backup root still succeeds.
findings.mitigation: Router is behind authMiddleware AND rbac(['admin']) (server.ts:533-536), so this is NOT unauthenticated/LAN-reachable. That is why severity is Medium, not Critical.
findings.correction_to_prior_audit: MOTARD_ERP_FULL_FORENSIC_AUDIT.md section 0 lists 'one unauthenticated LAN-reachable arbitrary-path restore (P1)'. That characterisation does NOT hold at this HEAD — the route is behind auth and admin RBAC. The path-restriction defect is real; the unauthenticated part is not.

findings.title: /settings/users CRUD mutates an in-memory array with no server call, so created users vanish on reload and can never authenticate
findings.evidence: addUser/updateUser/deleteUser (useSettings.ts:417-442) push to settings.users, call logActivity() and notify() — no persistSection(). Every OTHER section persists (:282 company, :307/318/326 units, :337/348/356 warehouses, :366/376/384 taxes, :394/404/412 paymentMethods, :450 company, :457 printing, :468 currencies); there is NO persistSection('users') anywhere. The backend allowlist (settings.route.ts:39-52) has no 'users' section either. The real routes POST/PATCH/DELETE /users and POST /users/:id/reset-password (user.route.ts:50,87,137,184) exist and are never called by the UI.
findings.actual: An admin adds a user, sees the success toast, and the row disappears on reload. The account cannot authenticate at all — it was never written to the users table the auth middleware reads. The in-memory SystemUser type carries a plaintext password?: string with no passwordHash, so even a hypothetical local login could not match the Argon2 hashes PasswordHasher produces.
findings.expected: The page calls the real user endpoints (list on load, PATCH on edit, POST + reset-password on create, DELETE on remove) so created users exist server-side and can log in; at minimum the page must not present itself as a working user manager.
findings.downstream_effects: An admin believes they have provisioned staff accounts; those staff cannot log in. In a multi-device deployment the phantom users exist in one browser only. Combined with F-016, the activity log records the creation as if it succeeded.
findings.reproduction: /settings/users -> add a user -> reload. The row is gone. Attempt to log in as that user -> rejected.
findings.recommended_fix: Wire the page to POST/PATCH/DELETE /users and POST /users/:id/reset-password; remove the plaintext password from SystemUser. Do NOT add 'users' to the settings allowlist — user records are tenant business data with their own routes.
findings.regression_risk: Medium — the screen currently drives off a synchronous in-memory list; server calls introduce loading and error states it does not render yet.
findings.regression_test: Add a user, reload, assert present; log in as that user and assert success.
findings.verified_by: lead auditor — CRUD functions, the full persistSection call-site list, the backend allowlist, the unused user routes, the SystemUser type and the login component all read directly.

findings.title: /settings/activity reads a module-scope array that is never persisted, so the audit trail is empty after refresh
findings.evidence: activity: [] as ActivityEntry[] (:198); logActivity unshifts into it and caps at 500 (:207-217) with no persistence; clearActivity wipes it (:473-476). loadSettings (:250-297) merges only company/units/taxes/warehouses/paymentMethods/currencies/printing — never activity. No activity settings section, no backend route. Backend DOES expose GET /sync/activity (sync.route.ts:452), unused by this page.
findings.actual: All 23 logActivity call sites write to a JS array discarded on reload. The page advertises the recent-actions trail but is empty after a refresh; the clear button destroys the rest behind a bare window.confirm.
findings.expected: Durable server-side per-tenant trail, or an explicit statement that the log is local and non-authoritative.
findings.downstream_effects: The audit trail an admin relies on for accountability silently does not exist after any reload.
findings.reproduction: Perform any settings action, reload /settings/activity — the entry is gone.
findings.recommended_fix: Persist activity server-side (GET /sync/activity already exists) or relabel the screen as a local session log.
findings.regression_test: Perform an action, reload, assert the entry survives.

findings.title: Invoice print-field visibility is written to localStorage and never replicates to other devices
findings.evidence: STORAGE_KEY = 'motard.invoice.printVisibility.v2' (:57); saveVisibility writes localStorage (:166-169). The same screen's printing block DOES persist (updatePrinting -> PUT /settings/printing, settings.invoice.tsx:117-124) and 'printing' is allowlisted (settings.route.ts:47) — so one screen mixes a replicated section with a local-only one.
findings.actual: Toggling field visibility writes one browser's localStorage. A second workstation or a reinstalled desktop prints every field.
findings.expected: Visibility belongs in the printing section so it replicates like paperSize and footerNote already do.
affected: the Sale/Entry/Return print components reading this local store
findings.downstream_effects: Print layout is inconsistent across devices with no indication why.
findings.reproduction: Hide a field on device A, print the same invoice on device B — the field appears.
findings.recommended_fix: Move visibility into the printing settings section.
findings.regression_risk: Low-medium — existing localStorage values need a one-time migration or they are lost.
findings.regression_test: Toggle visibility, reload on a second device profile, assert the setting replicates.

findings.title: Settings forms seed useState from built-in defaults before the server GET resolves, so an early save overwrites persisted values
findings.evidence: useSettings(); const [c, setC] = useState({ ...settings.company }); — seeded from built-in defaults. useSettings() fires loadSettings() in an effect which awaits getSettings() and then REPLACES settings.company/settings.printing. Local useState is never re-synced; no effect is keyed on the loaded object.
findings.actual: If the operator types and presses save before the GET returns (a few hundred ms on a cold desktop start), updateCompany/updatePrinting PUTs the hard-coded defaults over the company's saved name, address, tax number and paper size. The page shows the typed text and a success toast while the stored record reverts.
findings.expected: Form state initialises from the loaded server value, or is re-seeded when the loaded object changes, before save is enabled.
findings.downstream_effects: Silent loss of company/printing configuration with a success toast — the worst kind of failure to diagnose.
findings.reproduction: On a cold start, open /settings/company and save immediately; compare the stored value afterwards.
findings.recommended_fix: Seed from the loaded value or re-seed on load; disable save until the GET resolves.
findings.regression_test: Save before the GET resolves and assert the persisted value is the typed one.

findings.title: closing.tsx refreshAll() omits invalidateFinancialViews, leaving cashbox/ledger/statement stale after a year close
findings.evidence: refreshAll() invalidates only ['closing-preview'], ['count-sheet'], ['inventory']; called from both close.mutate onSuccess (:88) and reopen.mutate onSuccess (:99). invalidateFinancialViews.ts:15-26 covers dashboard, cashbox, ledger, profit, statement, party, parties, invoices plus refreshParties(). Project rule: frontend money mutations must call invalidateFinancialViews(qc).
findings.actual: After closing — the operation that freezes the books and the closing cashbox balances — the cashbox, ledger, statement, profit, dashboard and party-balance caches keep serving pre-close numbers until something else invalidates them.
findings.expected: refreshAll() calls invalidateFinancialViews(qc) alongside the count-sheet/inventory keys.
affected: every screen reading ['cashbox'], ['ledger'], ['statement'], ['parties'] after a close
findings.downstream_effects: Stale financial figures shown immediately after the books are frozen.
findings.reproduction: Close a year, then open the cashbox or statement screen without a full reload.
findings.regression_test: Close a year and assert the cashbox/ledger caches refetch.

positive_findings.title: npm audit is clean; the older audit's 14/10 vulnerability counts are resolved
positive_findings.note: MOTARD_ERP_FULL_FORENSIC_AUDIT.md records 14 root + 10 backend vulns. Production profile now reports zero; dev-dependency profile NOT re-run and not claimed clean.

positive_findings.title: Schema and journal parity hold across both engines
positive_findings.evidence: PG 47 tables / SQLite 52 (5 SQLite-only are the documented desktop-only set: drive-archive, financial-operation, motard-meta, sync-conflict, sync-tombstone). Zero column differences across the 47 shared tables. PG 103 .sql / 103 journal entries; SQLite 6 / 6 — both resolve exactly.
positive_findings.note: Independently corroborated by a second agent's database-layer audit with identical counts.

positive_findings.title: The two-engine repository twin discipline holds across all 37 pairs
positive_findings.evidence: Semantic-difference extractor over every Postgres*Repository.ts / sqlite/Sqlite*Repository.ts pair, normalising imports/comments/PORTED-FROM headers/whitespace, comparing behavioural signals (assert*, record*/compute*/notify*, runInTransaction/withTenantTx/sqliteDb/sqliteIndependentDb, orderBy(...), .limit(...), round2dp/round4dp/normalizeMoney2dp, idempotency refs, keyset helpers): 0 of 37 pairs diverge. Raw line counts differ by 29-87 per pair but every difference is import style, comment text, or drizzle dialect syntax.
positive_findings.actual: No behavioural divergence between engines at the repository layer.
positive_findings.downstream_effects: Rules cannot silently exist in one engine only.
positive_findings.reproduction: Run the semantic signal diff over repositories/ vs repositories/sqlite/.
positive_findings.existing_test_coverage: backend/tests/schema-migration-parity.test.ts exists but is NOT executed by CI (see F-001).
positive_findings.caveat: Proves the same functions are CALLED; does not prove their bodies are byte-identical, so a logic change inside a shared helper would not surface.

verified_sound.false_positive_note: Comparing against main-window.json alone flags 6 commands as ACL-dead. Wrong: Tauri ACL keys are hyphenated while Rust commands are underscored, and those six (recovery_*, startup_*) are granted by the separate recovery-window capability. Normalise underscores->hyphens and union all capability files.
